Concise Clinical Note

Consult Summary:
39-year-old man with sudden-onset, severe left-sided headache since 05:30 today; features most consistent with migraine vs. tension-type headache. No red-flag symptoms elicited. Started on ibuprofen and advised on stress reduction, hydration, sleep, and 1-week follow-up.

History:
• Presenting complaint: Woke at 05:30 with severe left-sided headache; constant and worse than any prior headaches.  
• Course: Persisting throughout day; mild relief after lying down; paracetamol ineffective.  
• Associated symptoms: Mild photophobia; brief morning dizziness now resolved. Denies neck stiffness, fever, nausea/vomiting, focal neurologic deficits.  
• Pertinent negatives: No previous migraines, no family migraine history.  
• Past medical history: Generalized anxiety disorder (≈2 y). No HTN or other chronic disease.  
• Allergies: NKDA.  
• Medications: Sertraline; single dose paracetamol today.  
• Social / preventive: Works long stressful hours (late nights ×2 mo). Lives with partner, non-smoker, runs 3×/week, owns a cat. Diet “okay.” No alcohol history discussed.

Examination:
Telephone consult—no vitals or physical examination possible.

Impression:
Most likely diagnoses:  
1. Migraine without aura – unilateral severe pain, photophobia, triggered by stress/sleep deprivation; poor response to paracetamol.  
2. Tension-type headache – chronic work stress and anxiety; prior milder frontal “band-like” headaches; partial relief with rest.  
Less likely but considered: cluster headache (lacks autonomic signs); subarachnoid hemorrhage (low probability but serious).

Plan:
• Pharmacologic: Start ibuprofen (first-line for migraine per current guidance; higher therapeutic dose). May continue paracetamol concurrently if needed.  
• Lifestyle / stress: Self-certified week off work; referral link for local counseling service to address work stress/anxiety.  
• Sleep & hydration: Target ≥7–8 h sleep nightly and ≥1.5–2 L water daily (excluding caffeine).  
• Education: Provide written information on headache “danger signs” and when to seek urgent care.  
• Follow-up: Telephone review in 1 week; earlier if headache worsens, new symptoms appear, or concerns arise. Possible blood tests or further assessment if no improvement.

Quality checks:
● Missing expected elements: no recorded vitals (BP, HR, temp); no neurological examination; alcohol intake not discussed.  
● Conflicts: None significant between transcript and DDx.  
● Transcript quality: Clear, complete history; limitations inherent to remote consult (no exam, vitals).
